title: Ukraine’s fiber-optic drones get squeezed by AI data center demand
gist: Fiber-optic FPV drones, immune to jamming, now consume a meaningful share of global optical fiber (Russia alone bought >10% of 2025 world output) just as AI data centers drive a projected 180 million km shortfall in 2026, pushing fiber prices up 6-10x for Ukrainian makers. BlueBird Tech describes how Ukrainian manufacturers are in-sourcing spooling and QA while remaining dependent on China, which favors Russian buyers.

themes.theme: Fiber demand collision: drones vs AI

insights.claim: Russia and Ukraine have been producing an estimated 50,000 fiber-optic drones per month, turning optical fiber into a one-time battlefield consumable.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Military consumption is a new, non-trivial and price-insensitive demand source for optical fiber.
insights.locator: Ukraine and Russia have been producing an estimated 50,000

insights.claim: Russia bought more than 60 million kilometers of fiber-optic cable in 2025, over 10 percent of global fiber production, versus never more than 1 percent of global demand previously.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: War-driven demand has structurally tightened the fiber market alongside AI — bullish for fiber producers' pricing power.
insights.locator: To get a better sense of how drone warfare has increased demand

insights.claim: TrendForce expects a worldwide optical fiber shortfall of 180 million kilometers in 2026 due to the AI data center buildout, raising costs for drone makers including for coveted bend-insensitive fiber.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Optical fiber is an AI supply-chain bottleneck; fiber and preform makers should see sustained pricing strength.
insights.locator: The global AI boom and ongoing data center buildout

insights.claim: BlueBird Tech reports fiber-optic material prices rose roughly six to 10 times between 2025 and 2026, with the worst prices and shortages around March before partial stabilization.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: A 6-10x input price spike signals extreme tightness in the fiber market and margin pressure for downstream users.
insights.quote: If we compare fiber-optic prices in 2025 and 2026, we have seen increases of roughly six to 10 times.

insights.claim: Chinese customs data show Russia imported 328,000 miles of fiber-optic cable from China in August 2025 versus just 72 miles for Ukraine, reflecting China's ties with Russia.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: China's selective supply gives Russia a material edge in a key drone input — a geopolitical lever over the war.
insights.locator: But China's economic and security ties with Russia

insights.claim: Despite intermediaries in other countries, China remains the main source of drone-grade fiber for Ukraine, and some Chinese manufacturers have refused Ukrainian buyers because they were from Ukraine.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Non-Chinese fiber supply chains for allied defense use are a strategic gap and potential opportunity for Western fiber makers.
insights.quote: There have also been cases where Chinese manufacturers have told Ukrainian buyers that they did not have material available for them because they were from Ukraine.
insights.locator: Ars Technica: Have Ukrainian companies experienced actual shortages

insights.claim: Ukrainian drone makers also rely on China for media converters, and face long transport routes, customs delays and air-raid interruptions that force joint production and logistics planning.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Multiple single-source dependencies on China extend beyond fiber in Ukraine's drone supply chain.
insights.locator: Fiber optic is also not the only component

insights.claim: Larger Ukrainian drone manufacturers are bringing spooling in-house, buying bulk fiber and winding their own drone spools to control quality and somewhat lower cost, while smaller firms still buy finished spools domestically or from China.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Vertical integration is consolidating Ukraine's drone industry toward larger, better-resourced producers.
insights.locator: Ars Technica: How are Ukrainian manufacturers adapting

insights.claim: Defects in Chinese-made finished spools motivated in-house spooling because a single spool defect can lose the drone, the mission and the target.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Quality control, not just price, is driving reshoring of drone subcomponent manufacturing.
insights.quote: If a fiber-optic spool has a defect, you can lose the drone, lose the mission, and lose the target.
insights.locator: But quality is the most important factor.

insights.claim: Fiber spool production requires skilled personnel with no formal training pipeline; training itself consumes many kilometers of fiber, and quality assurance needs link tests on every spool plus flight tests on samples from each batch.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Skills and QA throughput, not just material, cap scaling of fiber-drone production.

insights.claim: Fiber-optic drones emit no RF control signal, making them undetectable by conventional RF detectors and immune to electronic-warfare jamming, but they cost more, fly differently and require specialized pilot training, so radio-controlled drones still dominate.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Dense EW environments drive adoption of wired drones, creating durable demand for fiber and counter-drone tech.
insights.quote: So today, both sides are using fiber-optic drones on the battlefield, but radio-controlled drones still make up the larger share overall.

insights.claim: Russia first fielded unjammable fiber-optic drones during Ukraine's 2024 Kursk incursion, and finished spools now let drones operate at dozens of miles and up to 100 kilometers in extreme cases.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Range growth means more fiber per drone, compounding military fiber demand.
